newsitem.title: INDIA: India says committed to telecoms market access.
newsitem.headline: India says committed to telecoms market access.

text.p: India said on Tuesday it was committed to opening up its telecommunications market despite reservations voiced when it agreed to a global telecoms deal at Geneva last weekend.

India was one of the 68 countries that joined the deal to liberalise the $600 billion telecoms market, but led five nations that secured exemptions from granting a uniform most favoured nation (MFN) status to all countries, officials said.

"We made it clear that our demand on MFN did not amount to denial of market access," A.V. Gokak, the chairman of India's Telecom Commission, told a news conference. Gokak led Indian negotiators at the Geneva conference.
Gokak said India also told the World Trade Organisation talks it would consider opening long distance telephone calls to competition in 1999 and its international call market in 2004.
He said increased competition in the telecoms sector was expected to result in cheaper call rates for Indian consumers.

"This is only looking forward to the future. For the short term there is no change," V. Ramanan, an analyst at Peregrine Securities in Bombay, said. "Basically, the uncertainty over competition for VSNL (state-run Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd) has been removed. It is a beneficial step for the industry."
VSNL has a monopoly on international telecommunication services and Internet access services in India.
The Geneva deal will chiefly affect voice operated telephone systems and networks, domestic and international data transmission, global fax communications, private telephones and mobile systems.

Officials said India did not agree to a uniform MFN status because there was no legal assurance that it would not be bound to lower accounting rates, which determine the amount a country receives from another for incoming international phone calls.
It was joined by Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Turkey.

Gokak said India wanted to ensure that accounting rates, which depend on volumes of calls made, continued to be governed by bilateral agreements worked out with each country, and also to prevent the matter possibly going to the WTO's dispute panel.
But India's accounting rates were bound to come down, Gokak said. "The writing is on the wall. It is only a question of how long you will take," he said.

"In the short term, the telecom pact does not mean anything big for India as VSNL continues to retain its monopoly in overseas telecommunciations," an analyst at a foreign securities firm in Bombay told Reuters.
India charges relatively high rates for long-distance calls and international calls, which officials say help in cross-subsidising local calls and the expansion of India's rural telephone network.
India threw open its basic telephone services to private firms and allowed foreign equity of up to 49 percent under an economic liberalisation programme that started in 1991.

But at the Geneva negotiations, India agreed to a binding commitment on foreign equity of only up to 25 percent. "We said we would not like to bind ourselves (in WTO) to anything beyond 25 percent," Gokak said.

India also agreed to a reference paper that called for the implementation of common rules on regulating the telecoms industry. New Delhi has already begun the process of setting up a statutory telecoms regulator.
The Geneva deal is not a formal accord signed by member nations, but is an agreement on liberalisation measures commonly agreed on. It would take effect next year in most countries.
